definition: Trust vs. mistrust (0–1) → Autonomy vs. shame/doubt (1–3) → Initiative vs. guilt (3–6) → Industry vs. inferiority (6–12) → Identity vs. role confusion (12–18) → Intimacy vs. isolation (young adult) → Generativity vs. stagnation (middle adult) → Integrity vs. despair (late adult).

Sensorimotor (0–2, object permanence) → Preoperational (2–7, egocentrism, symbolic play, no conservation) → Concrete operational (7–11, conservation, logical thought about concrete things) → Formal operational (11+, abstract/hypothetical reasoning).
Preceded by normal autism and symbiosis. Then: Differentiation/hatching (5–10 mo) → Practicing (10–16 mo) → Rapprochement (16–24 mo, clinging/pushing away) → Object constancy (24–36 mo).

Secure: upset at separation, easily comforted at reunion. Avoidant: little distress, ignores caregiver on return. Ambivalent/resistant: very distressed, clingy yet angry, hard to soothe. Disorganized (Main): contradictory or fearful behavior; linked to maltreatment.
Preconventional (avoid punishment; self-interest) → Conventional (good boy/girl approval; law and order) → Postconventional (social contract; universal ethical principles).
Oral (0–1) → Anal (1–3) → Phallic (3–6, Oedipal conflict) → Latency (6–puberty) → Genital (puberty+).
Redirecting feelings from the real (threatening) target to a safer substitute. Example: angry at the boss, yells at the kids.

Projection: attributing your own unacceptable feelings to someone else. Projective identification: projecting feelings onto someone and then behaving in ways that lead them to actually feel or act that way.
Turning an unacceptable impulse into its exaggerated opposite (e.g., excessive sweetness toward someone you resent).
Channeling unacceptable impulses into socially acceptable activities (e.g., aggression into competitive sports). Considered a mature defense.
An action meant to symbolically cancel out an unacceptable thought or act (e.g., buying flowers after an angry outburst; seen in OCD rituals).
Microsystem (immediate settings) → Mesosystem (links between microsystems) → Exosystem (indirect settings, e.g., parent's job) → Macrosystem (culture, policy) → Chronosystem (change over time).
Equifinality: different starts → same outcome. Multifinality: same start → different outcomes.

Differentiation of self, triangles, nuclear family emotional process, family projection process, multigenerational transmission, emotional cutoff, sibling position, societal emotional process. Tool: genogram.
Denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance. Not strictly linear; people move back and forth.
Integration (keep origin culture + adopt host), Assimilation (adopt host, drop origin), Separation (keep origin, reject host), Marginalization (neither).
At least 2 weeks, 5+ of 9 symptoms, including depressed mood or anhedonia.
At least 2 years in adults (1 year in children/adolescents); never symptom-free for more than 2 months.

term: DSM duration: Manic vs. hypomanic episode
definition: Manic: at least 1 week (any duration if hospitalized); marked impairment or psychosis possible. Hypomanic: at least 4 consecutive days; no marked impairment, psychosis, or hospitalization.

term: Bipolar I vs. Bipolar II vs. Cyclothymia
definition: Bipolar I: at least one manic episode. Bipolar II: at least one hypomanic AND one major depressive episode, never manic. Cyclothymia: 2+ years (1 in youth) of hypomanic and depressive symptoms not meeting full episode criteria.
Brief psychotic disorder: 1 day to under 1 month. Schizophreniform: 1 to under 6 months. Schizophrenia: 6+ months (with at least 1 month of active symptoms).
A major mood episode concurrent with schizophrenia symptoms, PLUS delusions/hallucinations for 2+ weeks without a mood episode during the lifetime of the illness.
ASD: 3 days to 1 month after trauma. PTSD: more than 1 month. PTSD 'with delayed expression' if full criteria are met 6+ months after the event.
Symptoms begin within 3 months of the stressor and resolve within 6 months after the stressor (or its consequences) ends.
At least 6 months of excessive worry, hard to control; 3+ of 6 symptoms in adults (only 1 in children).
Recurrent unexpected panic attacks, plus at least 1 month of persistent worry about more attacks or maladaptive behavior change. Rule out medical causes first.
Typically 6 months or more.
Several symptoms before age 12, in 2+ settings. 6+ symptoms of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity for 6+ months (5+ if 17 or older).

ODD: 6+ months of angry/irritable mood, argumentative/defiant behavior, vindictiveness. Conduct disorder: violating others' rights (aggression, destruction, deceit/theft, serious rule violations) over 12 months.
Age 18+, evidence of conduct disorder before age 15, pervasive disregard for others' rights.
A (odd/eccentric): paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal. B (dramatic/erratic): antisocial, borderline, histrionic, narcissistic. C (anxious/fearful): avoidant, dependent, obsessive-compulsive.

Delirium: acute onset (hours to days), fluctuating attention and awareness, often reversible, medical emergency. Dementia (major neurocognitive disorder): gradual onset, progressive, attention preserved early.
Circumstantial: overly detailed but eventually reaches the point. Tangential: drifts off and never gets back to the point.
Vomiting, diarrhea, coarse tremor, confusion, ataxia, slurred speech. Get immediate medical attention. Dehydration and NSAIDs raise levels.

term: Tardive dyskinesia vs. NMS vs. akathisia
definition: TD: late, involuntary face/tongue movements after long-term antipsychotics. NMS: acute emergency (fever, rigidity, altered mental status, autonomic instability). Akathisia: inner restlessness, can't sit still.
Excess serotonergic activity (e.g., combining SSRIs/MAOIs/triptans): agitation, hyperthermia, sweating, tremor, muscle twitching (clonus), diarrhea. Medical emergency.
Alcohol and benzodiazepines/sedatives (seizures, delirium tremens). Requires medical supervision. Opioid withdrawal is miserable but rarely life-threatening by itself.

term: Anorexia vs. bulimia vs. binge-eating disorder
definition: Anorexia: significantly low weight, fear of gaining weight. Bulimia: binges + compensatory behaviors, at least weekly for 3 months, usually normal weight. BED: binges at least weekly for 3 months with distress, no regular compensatory behavior.
Based on adaptive functioning (conceptual, social, practical), NOT IQ score. Onset during the developmental period.
Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound.
Ideation, plan, intent, means/access, timeline, past attempts, protective factors. Ask directly; asking does not increase risk.

term: Somatic symptom vs. illness anxiety vs. factitious vs. malingering
definition: SSD: distressing physical symptoms + excessive thoughts about them. Illness anxiety: fear of illness, minimal symptoms. Factitious: faking for the sick role (internal motive). Malingering: faking for external gain (not a mental disorder).
Precontemplation → Contemplation → Preparation → Action → Maintenance (and relapse/recycling). Match the intervention to the stage.
Open-ended questions, Affirmations, Reflections, Summaries. Elicit change talk; roll with resistance; avoid the 'righting reflex.'

All-or-nothing thinking, overgeneralization, mental filter, disqualifying the positive, mind reading, fortune telling, catastrophizing, emotional reasoning, 'should' statements, labeling, personalization.
Mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness. Developed by Linehan for chronic suicidality and BPD.
Systematic desensitization: relaxation + gradual fear hierarchy (reciprocal inhibition). Flooding: immediate, prolonged exposure to the most feared stimulus.
First-line psychotherapy for OCD: exposure to triggers while blocking compulsions.

Positive reinforcement: add something good. Negative reinforcement: remove something bad (both increase behavior). Positive punishment: add something bad. Negative punishment: remove something good (both decrease behavior). Extinction: stop reinforcing.
Miracle question, exception questions, scaling questions, coping questions, compliments. Focus on solutions and strengths, not problem history.
White & Epston. Externalizing the problem, deconstructing dominant stories, finding unique outcomes, re-authoring.
Focuses on boundaries (enmeshed ↔ disengaged), subsystems, and hierarchy. Techniques: joining, enactment, restructuring, family mapping.
Focuses on problem-maintaining interaction patterns. Techniques: directives, paradoxical interventions (prescribing the symptom), reframing.
Forming → Storming → Norming → Performing → Adjourning. Boston model (Garland, Jones & Kolodny): preaffiliation, power and control, intimacy, differentiation, separation.
Assess safety and lethality first, then establish rapport, identify the major problem, explore feelings, generate alternatives, make an action plan, follow up (Roberts' 7-stage model).

Transference: client redirects feelings about significant others onto the worker. Countertransference: worker's own reactions to the client. Manage countertransference through self-awareness and supervision.
Safety; trustworthiness and transparency; peer support; collaboration and mutuality; empowerment, voice, and choice; cultural, historical, and gender issues.
Criticism, hostility, emotional overinvolvement in families. High EE predicts relapse in schizophrenia. Intervention: family psychoeducation.
Reducing negative consequences of behavior without requiring abstinence (e.g., naloxone, syringe services, medication for opioid use disorder). Meets clients where they are.
Assessment, planning, linkage/referral, monitoring, advocacy, evaluation.
Service, social justice, dignity and worth of the person, importance of human relationships, integrity, competence.
When a client makes a credible threat of serious harm to an identifiable person, the worker must take reasonable steps to protect them (warn, notify police, hospitalize). Specifics vary by state.
Subpoena: must respond, but don't release records without client consent; assert privilege. Court order: must comply, but may ask the court to limit disclosure or seal the records.
Reasonable suspicion of child (and, by state law, elder/dependent adult) abuse. Proof is not required, and the worker should not investigate.
First consult with the colleague when feasible and help them take remedial action. If that doesn't work, go through appropriate channels (employer, NASW, licensing board).

Never with current clients. Not with clients' relatives/close others if there's risk of harm. Former clients: should not, due to potential harm; the worker bears the full burden. Workers always set the boundaries.
Avoid. Acceptable only if it's a community norm, essential to services, negotiated without coercion, and initiated by the client with informed consent. The worker bears the burden.
Provide reasonable access. Limit only in exceptional circumstances with compelling evidence of serious harm; document the request and the reason.
Permitted if financial arrangements were made clear, the client is not an imminent danger, and the consequences were discussed.
Purpose of services, risks, limits due to third-party payers, costs, reasonable alternatives, right to refuse or withdraw, timeframe. Use clear language; use a qualified interpreter if needed.
Avoid when there is risk of exploitation or harm. When unavoidable (e.g., rural practice), the worker sets clear, appropriate, culturally sensitive boundaries.
Respect clients' right to choose, except when their actions pose a serious, foreseeable, and imminent risk to themselves or others.
Kept separate from the medical record. They get extra protection: most disclosures require specific client authorization, and clients don't have the same right of access as to the main record.
Federal rule giving extra confidentiality protection to records from federally assisted substance use disorder programs.

Priority order when principles conflict: 1) protection of life, 2) social justice/equality, 3) autonomy and freedom, 4) least harm, 5) quality of life, 6) privacy and confidentiality, 7) truthfulness and full disclosure.
